canonical_statement: The CURE trial compared the efficacy and safety of early and long-term clopidogrel plus aspirin with aspirin alone in patients with acute coronary syndromes without ST-segment elevation.

Eligible patients were hospitalized within 24 hours after symptom onset without ST-segment elevation; after the first 3000 patients, enrollment required either electrocardiographic changes or elevated cardiac enzymes or markers at entry.

canonical_statement: Key exclusions were contraindications to antithrombotic or antiplatelet therapy, high bleeding risk or severe heart failure, oral anticoagulant use, coronary revascularization within the previous 3 months, or intravenous glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitor use within the previous 3 days.

canonical_statement: CURE was a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial using central 24-hour computerized allocation with permuted blocks stratified by clinical center.
Follow-up assessments occurred at discharge, at 1 and 3 months, and then every 3 months until study end.
The first primary outcome was the composite of cardiovascular death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, or stroke.

concept.text: Cardiovascular death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, or stroke

canonical_statement: The second primary outcome was the first primary composite plus refractory ischemia.

concept.text: Cardiovascular death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, stroke, or refractory ischemia

canonical_statement: Secondary efficacy outcomes were severe ischemia, heart failure, and need for revascularization; safety outcomes were bleeding complications categorized as life-threatening, major, or minor.

concept.text: Secondary efficacy and bleeding safety outcomes

canonical_statement: All primary outcomes and life-threatening and major bleeding complications were adjudicated by persons unaware of treatment assignment.
Efficacy analyses used the intention-to-treat principle; log-rank or chi-square tests were used, and subgroup interactions were tested in Cox regression models.
Vital status was ascertained for 12,549 of 12,562 randomized patients (99.9%); 6 clopidogrel and 7 placebo patients were lost to follow-up.

canonical_statement: During the study, 43.7% underwent angiography, 16.5% CABG, and 21.2% PTCA; study medication was frequently interrupted around revascularization and open-label thienopyridines were permitted when clinically indicated.
The trial primarily included centers without a routine policy of early invasive management, which limits direct applicability to settings built around routine early invasive strategies.
Frequent interruption of randomized therapy around PTCA/CABG and use of open-label thienopyridines could attenuate the observed contrast between randomized groups.

The investigators concluded that adding clopidogrel to aspirin reduced the composite of cardiovascular death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, or stroke and related ischemic events, but increased bleeding risk.
The trial was supported by Sanofi-Synthelabo and Bristol-Myers Squibb.
Yusuf, Mehta, Tognoni, and Fox reported receiving honoraria for educational activities or serving as consultants to Bristol-Myers Squibb and Sanofi-Synthelabo.
